questions.q: Why does converting from CSV to Parquet typically reduce bytes scanned for narrow queries on wide tables?
options: Parquet is columnar, so a query needing only some columns reads just those columns instead of every column in every row
Parquet files are always physically smaller regardless of what's queried
Parquet removes the need for a WHERE clause
CSV files cannot be queried by Athena at all
questions.explain: Columnar storage lets a query read only the specific columns it needs, unlike row-oriented CSV/JSON where every column of every row is read together.

questions.q: Why does columnar storage make compression more effective?
options: Values within a single column tend to be more similar to each other than values across a mixed row, compressing better when stored contiguously
Compression only works on columnar formats and never on row-oriented ones
Columnar formats disable compression entirely
It has no relationship to compression effectiveness
questions.explain: Storing similar values (like repeated IDs or statuses) contiguously by column allows more effective compression than mixed row data.

questions.q: How do partitioning, columnar format, and compression relate to each other for Athena cost?
options: They stack — partitioning controls which files open, columnar format controls how much of each file is read, compression shrinks the physical bytes read
They are competing alternatives, and only one can be used at a time
Only partitioning has any effect on Athena billing; format and compression don't matter
Compression must be disabled for partitioning to work
questions.explain: These three techniques address different parts of the same cost equation and compound together rather than substituting for each other.

questions.q: What is the standard Glue job pattern this lesson describes for applying these optimizations?
options: Read raw CSV, partition it by a sensible key, and write it out as compressed Parquet
Delete all raw data immediately after it lands in S3
Convert Parquet back into CSV for archival
Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE as the only step needed
questions.explain: A common real pattern is a Glue ETL job that transforms raw CSV into partitioned, compressed Parquet.

questions.q: A table is already well partitioned but still stored as uncompressed CSV. Has all available cost savings been captured?
options: No — converting to compressed, columnar Parquet is still available and stacks on top of partitioning's savings
Yes, partitioning alone captures the maximum possible savings
No further optimization is ever possible once a table is partitioned
Compression would actually increase Athena's bytes-scanned cost
questions.explain: Partitioning is only one of three independent levers; format and compression remain available savings on top of it.
